canonical_topic: PJM (Mid-Atlantic) power market geography and fundamentals
definition: PJM's service territory spans a geographically and climatically diverse part of the Mid-Atlantic, which produces different marginal fuels and demand patterns across its western and eastern halves.
core_idea: In the western part of PJM, cheap native coal from Pennsylvania and West Virginia sets the marginal price of power, while gas-fired generation is the marginal price setter on the East Coast and in Virginia. Climate ranges from cold winters/hot summers in the north to milder winters and longer hot summers in the south.
key_points: Western PJM's marginal fuel is coal, sourced locally from Pennsylvania and West Virginia.
Eastern PJM (East Coast, Virginia) relies on gas-fired plants as the marginal price setter.
Climate varies north-to-south: the north sees cold winters and hot summers; the south has milder winters and extended hot summers.
Many power plants sit in sparsely populated parts of the PJM footprint and export power into denser, higher-demand areas.
This generation-to-load geography routinely creates congestion on the transmission lines linking rural generation areas to population centers.
relationships: Generation-load geographic mismatch drives transmission congestion, a recurring theme across US ISOs (see MISO, ERCOT).
trading_implications: Coal prices are a leading indicator for western PJM power prices; gas prices matter more for eastern/Virginia nodes.
Congestion between exporting rural generation zones and importing population centers creates locational basis risk.
caveats: Assuming a single marginal fuel applies uniformly across all of PJM, when in practice it differs materially between the western (coal) and eastern (gas) sub-regions.
